owner: src/spine/lever.py -- and nothing else. No other file in the tree was edited by me; src/spine/derive.py and tests/test_fabric.py show as modified in git status because another agent was editing them concurrently during this run.
summary: THREE MECHANISMS LANDED IN src/spine/lever.py, ALL THREE DRIVEN AND PASTED. (1) REFUSE_NON_FINITE_FLOAT, a module constant with a full docstring in D17's settled shape, refusing nan/inf/-inf on a FLOAT lever inside Lever.coerce in this file's own refusal idiom. Its scope claim was VERIFIED before it was relied on, not assumed: 110 int levers x 9 non-finite spellings = 990 cells, 0 accepted, with the floor OFF as well as on -- int levers never needed it and the floor does not reach them; the same 9 spellings on the 97 floats = 873 cells, all accepted before and all refused after. I also found and closed the one route around it: a float LITERAL default never passes through coerce, so the same rule is stated at declaration under the same switch (0 of 97 levers affected today). (2) domain=(lo, hi), an optional kwarg in the shape choices= already has -- checked at declaration against the lever's own default, checked in coerce after coercion, LeverError naming the generated env name and the value. EITHER END MAY BE None and hi=None is the COMMON case (163 of 207 get no ceiling under an honest population) and ADMITS +inf, which is written in the declaration comment because it is the reason the floor exists: the two are COMPLEMENTS, and domain= alone would leave +inf legal on the 53 open-topped floats. THE INTERVAL IS CLOSED AT BOTH ENDS -- decided, and justified from the 33 levers about to be populated, where both endpoints are values somebody configures (OPT_LR_DECAY=1.0 is accepted BY NAME by opt/api.py today) and where an exclusive end would REFUSE a value a shipped body accepts. A declaration needing an OPEN end writes the closed pair that CONTAINS its interval and keeps the strict clause at the read site: the declaration under-refuses by one endpoint and never over-refuses. An int lever's endpoints must be ints and no endpoint may be infinite, because domain=(0.0, inf) would admit the +inf the floor refuses. (3) REFUSE_INEXACT_INT, one rule closing BOTH live holes at that line: an int lever resolves to the integer its string denotes, or it is refused. I chose LOSSLESSNESS over NOTATION -- '8.0' and '1e3' are integers written as floats and resolve normally; '0.4' is refused because 0 is not 0.4, and '1e26' is refused because the tree cannot DELIVER 1e26, not because 1e26 is large. The textual alternative was refused for a measured reason: it would refuse '1e3' and '8.0' and still ACCEPT '1e26'. WHAT IT BREAKS, SCANNED NOT ESTIMATED: 1093 int-lever assignment sites in 78 files across src/, tests/, tools/, docs/ and the root scripts, and exactly ONE is non-exact -- MEM_QUOTA=0.4, in a comment describing this very defect. Nothing that runs today breaks. NOTHING HERE MAKES ANY LEVER HARMLESS AND NO DOCSTRING SAYS IT DOES: OPT_LR=1e6 is finite, passes every rule above, and leaves every parameter at -3928. The file says so in three places. 13 prose sites in 8 files -- three of them inside raised operator-facing messages -- assert 'a Lever has no range facility' as a load-bearing premise and are now false; every one has an exact text-anchored find/replace in unfinished, written to PRESERVE the three standing U.FRACTION rulings rather than disturb them.

It fires after the type coercion and before choices= and domain=, on the FLOAT branch only. The message names the raw string AND what it read as ('1e999' reads as inf), says the refusal is about the SPELLING and makes no claim about any other value of the lever, and names the constant to flip. 873 cells (97 float levers x 9 non-finite spellings) go from accepted to refused; 0 other cells move.

findings.item: PART 1 -- THE SWITCH: a module-level constant with a full docstring, per D17's settled shape
findings.detail: REFUSE_NON_FINITE_FLOAT = True, a module constant carrying a docstring that states what it governs (the 97 floats, measured), why the first read, WHAT TURNING IT OFF COSTS, what it does not buy, and what would change the answer. The carrier follows src/ckpt/api.py::REFUSE_NEGATIVE_PERIOD, and the banner above records two reasons that are STRONGER here than there: (a) a lever cannot carry this at all -- the rule runs inside coerce, before any Config exists, so the only environment form is a raw os.environ read, which is legal in this one file and is refused anyway because it would be the tree's first environment name that is not a lever, invisible to registry/census/04_LEVERS, i.e. exactly the failure this module's header exists to end; (b) the assembly latches after one build, so a lever switch needs a fresh process per arm while a constant flips in one. THE COST IS STATED, NOT DISCOVERED: turning it off is a code edit, not an environment variable, and an operator holding only a shell cannot reach it -- the same D17 gap docs/04_CONTRACT.md already records for the five periods.
findings.repro: prove.py section D drives ONE declaration with the constant True then False, and section F drives BOTH arms over the whole registry. With REFUSE_NON_FINITE_FLOAT = False: 388 of 2691 cells change, ALL 388 REFUSED->accepted, 0 change any other way; levers touched 97; values touched ['-inf','1e999','inf','nan']. findings.item: PART 1 -- THE ONE ROUTE AROUND THE FLOOR, FOUND AND CLOSED AT THE OTHER DOOR
findings.detail: from_env does not call coerce when the environment does not name the lever -- it uses the declared default directly. So a literal Lever(float('inf'), ...) would reach a frozen Config having passed no rule, and the four package loops that scan for a non-finite lever (fabric, sig, opt, tok) would be the only readers standing. The same rule is now stated once more at declaration time, answering to the SAME constant. Measured: 0 of the 97 float levers declares a non-finite default today, so it refuses nothing that exists.

A default is the one value from_env never coerces, so spine/lever.py::REFUSE_NON_FINITE_FLOAT cannot see it at resolution time and it would reach a frozen Config unexamined. ; default float('nan'), floor ON -> REFUSED ; default 0.5, floor ON -> 'DECLARED' ; default float('inf'), floor OFF -> 'DECLARED'. Registry scan: float levers with a NON-FINITE declared default: 0 [].

findings.item: PART 2 -- domain=(lo, hi) ON THE Lever DECLARATION, in the shape choices= already has

findings.item: PART 2 DESIGN POINT -- EITHER END MAY BE None, AND hi=None IS THE COMMON CASE AND ADMITS +inf
findings.detail: Written down in the declaration comment with the counts that force it: of the 207 numeric levers the HIGH end is obvious on 44, is another lever or a wire on 15 (LM_CTX <= d_pos_max, WORLD_N0 <= WORLD_NMAX, MEM_KEY_DEPTH <= LM_LAYERS -- none expressible as a per-lever pair), is a ceiling this tree has explicitly declined to set on 16, and is NOT DERIVABLE AT ALL on 131. The comment states that hi=None ADMITS +inf, that this is why the floor exists, and that the two are COMPLEMENTS AND NOT ALTERNATIVES because domain= alone would leave +inf legal on the 53 open-topped float levers -- OPT_LR, OPT_WEIGHT_DECAY, SIG_VAR_WEIGHT, SIG_COV_WEIGHT, FAB_ROUTE_T among them. It also says, in as many words, that a domain is NOT a statement that the lever is harmless at every value it admits.

FLOOR ON: '1.0'->1.0 '0.0'->0.0 '1e26'->1e+26 ; '-0.5' REFUSED by the DOMAIN ; 'nan','inf','-inf' REFUSED by the FLOOR. Section H reproduces the audit's four-row table on the shipped file with the floor off, so every refusal shown is the DOMAIN's own: (0.0,1.0) nan/inf/-inf/1e26 all REFUSED, 0 and 0.5 pass; (0.0,None) inf=pass 1e26=pass; (None,1.0) -inf=pass; (1,None) 0=REFUSED 0.5=REFUSED.

findings.item: PART 2 DESIGN POINT -- THE INTERVAL IS CLOSED AT BOTH ENDS, justified from the 33, with the open-end fallback written down
findings.detail: DECIDED CLOSED. Justification recorded in the declaration comment and drawn from the 33 levers about to be populated (.rework/audits/options_domain.json, option-(3) finding): that list is probabilities (LM_DROPOUT, TOK_DROPOUT, MEM_WRITE_GATE, FAB_MUT_BIG_P), shares and quantiles (FAB_CULL_FRAC, DOM_RADIUS_Q, MEM_PROBATION_FRAC, DATA_HOLDOUT_FRAC) and three already refused at both ends by hand in src/opt/api.py::build. On that population BOTH endpoints are values somebody configures: 0.0 is 'never' and is a declared or measured-legitimate value on 46 of the 207, and 1.0 is 'always' -- src/opt/api.py::build already accepts OPT_LR_DECAY=1.0 BY NAME. An exclusive end would REFUSE a value a shipped body accepts, which is the one direction of error that breaks a configuration that works. A count's lo=1 has to be inclusive or no count lever can be set to 1. The two levers whose natural low end is NEGATIVE (EVAL_GENUINE_SIL, a silhouette in [-1,1]; MEM_MATCH_FLOOR, a cosine similarity) make the same point: both endpoints are attainable readings and a reflexive lo=0.0 is simply wrong. WHAT A DECLARATION NEEDING AN OPEN END DOES INSTEAD, written down: it writes the CLOSED pair that CONTAINS its interval -- domain=(0.0, 1.0) for the half-open [0.0, 1.0) that src/lm/api.py::resolve and src/opt/api.py::build both need -- and keeps the strict clause at the read site, where the mechanism is and the message can say why. The declaration then under-refuses by exactly one endpoint and never over-refuses: a domain is the OUTERMOST interval the declaration alone can defend, not the tightest the mechanism has. The comment also records that this forecloses nothing -- a later inclusivity field would NARROW what a declaration can say, so every closed pair written today would still mean what it says -- and forbids faking a strict end by nudging an endpoint, because 'greater than 0.0' and 'at least 5e-324' are not the same sentence.
findings.repro: prove.py section C: both endpoints accepted on every populated domain -- ZZ_LR_DECAY '0.0'->0.0 and '1.0'->1.0 ; ZZ_GENUINE_SIL '-1.0'->-1.0 and '1.0'->1.0 ; ZZ_RANK '1'->1. The values just outside are refused: '-0.0001', '1.0001', '-1.5', '0', '-3'.

findings.item: PART 2 DESIGN POINT -- THE DEFAULT IS CHECKED AGAINST ITS OWN DOMAIN AT DECLARATION TIME
findings.detail: As choices= does, and for the sharper reason that the default is the ONE value from_env never coerces: a default outside its own domain could not be refused at resolution time at all, so it is refused where it is written. The message cannot quote the env name (Lever.__init__ runs before __set_name__, so the lever does not yet know its field name or its owner's prefix -- the same constraint choices= has); it quotes the default and the domain, which locates the line. _domain_ends also refuses the other declaration-time errors a pair can carry.
findings.repro: prove.py section E: default 2.0 in (0.0,1.0) -> REFUSED: default 2.0 is outside its own domain [0.0, 1.0]. A default no environment can reproduce is the one configuration this tree cannot refuse at resolution time -- from_env never coerces it -- so it is refused at declaration. ; default 0 in (1,None) -> REFUSED ... outside its own domain [1, unbounded] ; default 0.5 in (0.0,1.0) -> DECLARED (no refusal) ; domain=(None,None) -> REFUSED (bounds nothing) ; lo above hi -> REFUSED (empty) ; infinite hi end -> REFUSED (an unbounded end is written None -- an infinite endpoint would ADMIT the infinity REFUSE_NON_FINITE_FLOAT exists to refuse) ; nan end -> REFUSED ; domain on a str lever -> REFUSED ; domain on a bool lever -> REFUSED ; choices outside domain -> REFUSED: choices [7.0] fall outside domain [0.0, 1.0] ; not a pair -> REFUSED.

findings.item: PART 2 DESIGN POINT -- int vs float: an int lever's domain cannot admit a float
findings.detail: An INT lever's endpoints must themselves be ints (bool excluded, since bool subclasses int): domain=(0.0, 1.0) on an int lever is refused at declaration, because an int lever resolves to an int and a fractional endpoint bounds nothing that can occur while reading as though fractional values were in play. The REVERSE is allowed and the comment says why: an int endpoint on a float lever compares exactly, and domain=(0, 1) on a rate is the same interval as (0.0, 1.0) with two fewer characters -- refusing it would be ceremony. Both ends must also be FINITE: domain=(0.0, inf) would admit +inf (inf <= inf), undoing the floor with a bound that looks like one; unboundedness is spelled None, which a reader can see.
findings.repro: prove.py section E: int lever, float ends -> REFUSED: domain lo=0.0 is a float on an INT lever (default 16). An int lever resolves to an int, so a fractional endpoint bounds nothing that can occur and states a range the lever does not have. Write the int you mean. ; float lever, int ends -> 'DECLARED (no refusal)' ; infinite hi end -> REFUSED ; nan end -> REFUSED.

findings.item: PART 3 HOLE A+B -- ONE RULE FOR BOTH: REFUSE_INEXACT_INT. '0.4' refused, '8.0' accepted, '1e26' refused
findings.detail: THE RULE I CHOSE IS LOSSLESSNESS, NOT NOTATION: an int lever resolves to the integer its string denotes, or it is refused. int(float(raw)) is two lossy steps and this refuses exactly when either loses something. '8.0' is an integer written as a float and survives exactly, so it resolves to 8; '1e3'->1000; '1_000' and ' 12 ' resolve as float() already reads them. '0.4' does not survive (0 is not 0.4) and neither does '1e26' (float cannot represent 10**26, so the value that runs is 4764729344 larger than the one typed). THE ALTERNATIVE I REFUSED, and why, is recorded in the docstring: a TEXTUAL rule (refuse any raw containing '.' or an exponent) would refuse '1e3' and '8.0', which denote integers exactly and which any harness writing str(x) from a computed value produces, AND it would still accept '1e26', because that string is spelled like an integer to a textual rule and is not one to the parser -- a rule that refuses correct values and admits the measured defect. IMPLEMENTATION: decimal.Decimal(raw) == int(float(raw)). Decimal parses the same grammar float() does (whitespace, sign, underscores, exponents) and carries the exact decimal value, so the comparison is between what was typed and what will run; where Decimal cannot parse a string float() accepted -- no such spelling is known -- the weaker test float(raw) == int(float(raw)) stands in. NOTE WHAT THIS DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO: it invents no magnitude ceiling. '1e26' is refused because the tree cannot DELIVER 1e26 on an int lever, not because 1e26 is too large -- '1152921504606846976' (2**60, exactly representable) resolves normally.
findings.repro: prove.py section B, through a real spine.assemble.build on MEM_REKEY_EVERY (declared default 200; 0 is its declared DISARM in src/memory/api.py::maintain): unset -> 200 ; '0' -> 0 ; '1' -> 1 ; '8' -> 8 ; '8.0' -> 8 ; '1e3' -> 1000 ; '2000' -> 2000 ; '0.4' -> REFUSED: MEM_REKEY_EVERY='0.4' does not denote the integer it resolves to (0). ... ; '0.9' -> REFUSED ... resolves to (0) ; '-0.5' -> REFUSED ... resolves to (0) ; '1e26' -> REFUSED: MEM_REKEY_EVERY='1e26' does not denote the integer it resolves to (100000000000000004764729344). ... ; 'nan' -> REFUSED: MEM_REKEY_EVERY='nan' is not a int ; 'inf' -> REFUSED: MEM_REKEY_EVERY='inf' is not a int (both of those unchanged, by the pre-existing OverflowError token).

findings.item: PART 3 -- WHAT THE INTEGRALITY RULE BREAKS, MEASURED ACROSS THE REPOSITORY RATHER THAN ESTIMATED
findings.detail: It is a behaviour change to all 110 int levers: any configuration setting one to a fractional or inexact-magnitude string now stops the build and says so by name instead of running at the truncated number. I scanned every assignment site of every int lever's env name in src/, tests/, tools/, docs/ and the root scripts -- 1093 sites in 78 files -- and exactly ONE is non-exact: MEM_QUOTA=0.4, which is PROSE in a comment in src/memory/api.py describing this very defect, not a configuration. No script, sweep, test or recorded configuration in the tree sets an int lever to a non-exact value. The same scan over float levers found 421 assignment sites and exactly 3 non-finite ones -- FAB_ROUTE_T=+inf in src/fabric/api.py and SIG_TEMP=-inf, SIG_WARMUP_MIN_FRAC=-inf in src/sig/api.py -- all three also prose describing the defect. So neither rule breaks anything that runs today. What DOES change for a reader is that those sweep findings are now refusals rather than results, and the prose describing them as live is stale -- listed under unfinished for the owners.
findings.repro: <scratch>/scan_uses.py over the working tree (runs/, .git/, archive/, data/ excluded): int-lever assignment sites found: 1093, distinct files: 78. NON-EXACT int-lever assignments (would newly refuse): 1 -- ('src/memory/api.py', 'MEM_QUOTA', '0.4'). float-lever assignment sites: 421, NON-FINITE ones (would newly refuse): 3 -- ('src/fabric/api.py','FAB_ROUTE_T','+inf'), ('src/sig/api.py','SIG_TEMP','-inf'), ('src/sig/api.py','SIG_WARMUP_MIN_FRAC','-inf'). Each of the four confirmed to be inside a comment by grep -n.

findings.item: TWO CONSTANTS AND NOT ONE, AND domain= GETS NEITHER -- the carrier decision, written down
findings.detail: The banner above the constants records it. The two rules govern DISJOINT populations (97 floats, 110 ints, measured, no lever in both) and answer different questions, so one shared flag would mean an operator turning off the rule that broke their run also turns off a rule that had nothing to do with it. domain= gets no switch at all because its blast radius is one lever and deleting the kwarg is the switch -- which is also what .rework/audits/options_domain.json's D17 finding concluded: a switch for a CENTRAL rule, none for a per-lever declaration.
findings.repro: prove.py section F drives each constant independently over the whole registry and shows the two arms touch disjoint value sets: REFUSE_NON_FINITE_FLOAT=False touches ['-inf','1e999','inf','nan'] on 97 levers; REFUSE_INEXACT_INT=False touches ['0.4','0.5','1e26'] on 110 levers. With BOTH False, 718 of 2691 cells differ from shipped = 388 + 330 exactly, i.e. the two arms do not overlap.

findings.item: THE INVERTED-CHAIN COMPARISON IN THE DOMAIN CHECK IS LOAD-BEARING, and says so
findings.detail: The domain test is written `not lo <= v` / `not v <= hi`, never `v < lo or v > hi`. Written the second way every comparison against nan is False and a nan PASSES a domain it is plainly outside; written the first way the same comparison is False and `not` makes it a refusal. That is the whole reason ANY finite endpoint refuses nan for free, and it is the grammar the opt sweep found separating the guards that held against NaN from the ones that did not -- there by accident, thirteen times; here on purpose, once, with a comment saying so.
findings.repro: prove.py section H with the floor OFF, so the refusals shown are the domain's alone: domain=(0.0,1.0) nan=REFUSED ; domain=(0.0,None) nan=REFUSED ; domain=(None,1.0) nan=REFUSED ; domain=(1,None) nan=REFUSED. Every row refuses nan; only the finite-high rows refuse inf.

findings.item: WHAT THE FLOOR COSTS THE FOUR PER-PACKAGE NON-FINITE REFUSALS -- stated, not hidden, and NOT removed
findings.detail: With REFUSE_NON_FINITE_FLOAT True, the four loop-shaped per-package refusals (src/fabric/api.py::build, src/sig/api.py::build, src/opt/api.py::build, src/tok/api.py::build_vocabulary) can no longer fire from a lever: each skips d_ wires and scans only float levers, and no float lever can now hold a non-finite value. They are NOT dead code and must not be deleted -- the switch turns the floor off, and a non-finite float default would have reached them before I closed that door too. But a reader should know they are unreachable at the shipped setting, which is the untrippable-guard class this tree names, and that is a sentence for their owners to write in their own files. Recorded under unfinished. src/data/api.py::data_plan's exposure check is the same case for its two levers.
